Fermion mass (mf​)

Words: 29
Standard Model OurBigBook.com
The rest mass of a fermion. In the Standard Model, charged-fermion masses arise from couplings to the Higgs field; at energies much greater than these masses, helicity and chirality can be related with small mass corrections.

Flavour mixing (ψα​=∑i​Uαi​ψi​)

Words: 83 Articles: 1
Standard Model OurBigBook.com
The interaction-labelled fields of several particle species can be linear combinations of the propagation or mass eigenfields. A unitary matrix relates orthonormal bases with canonical kinetic normalization. Quark mixing is described by the CKM matrix; the lepton mixing matrix describes the corresponding mismatch for leptons. A mixing angle parametrizes part of this matrix once ordering and phase conventions are fixed.

Mixing angle (θ)

Words: 33
Flavour mixing OurBigBook.com
An angle parametrizing a rotation between interaction and propagation bases. Examples include the Cabibbo angle and the three angles in the lepton mixing matrix. The value must be associated with a specified matrix parametrization and basis ordering.

Strong interaction

Words: 344 Articles: 7
Standard Model OurBigBook.com
The strong interaction is the SU(3)c​ gauge interaction described by Quantum chromodynamics. It couples quarks and gluons through color charge.

OZI rule

Words: 49
Strong interaction OurBigBook.com
Hadronic processes with disconnected quark-flavour lines are often suppressed relative to connected quark rearrangement. A predominantly strange phi meson can decay to kaons through light-pair creation while its original strange lines survive, whereas a purely pionic final state requires strange-pair annihilation. The rule is an approximate dynamical pattern, not an exact conservation law.

Hadronic final-state interaction

Words: 87 Articles: 1
Strong interaction OurBigBook.com
An interaction among outgoing hadrons that changes the observed channel amplitude or its phase after the short-distance production vertex. Rescattering can mix channels with the same conserved quantum numbers. Consequently identical CKM suppression orders do not imply equal branching fractions, and a free-quark spectator diagram need not determine the ordering of exclusive hadronic decay rates.

Strong phase (δ)

Words: 35
Hadronic final-state interaction OurBigBook.com
A phase in a hadronic matrix element generated by strong interaction dynamics, including rescattering of final states. It does not change sign under conjugation of the weak coupling constant. Interference measurements depend on relative strong phases, rather than their common overall value.

Quark-line flavour rearrangement

Words: 54
Strong interaction OurBigBook.com
A quark-line diagram can show how existing valence quarks are regrouped into outgoing hadrons while gluons exchange momentum and colour. Alternatively, a quark-antiquark pair can annihilate and create a different flavour pair with zero net flavour. Such drawings enforce global charge, baryon number and flavour constraints; they are not controlled perturbative calculations of an exclusive low-energy hadronic amplitude because binding is nonperturbative.

Meson-baryon scattering

Words: 135 Articles: 2
Strong interaction OurBigBook.com
Scattering with one meson and one baryon in the initial and final states. The strong interaction conserves electric charge, baryon number, net strangeness, four-momentum, total angular momentum, and parity. Approximate isospin symmetry imposes additional relations among charge-channel amplitudes.

Strangeness selection in pion-proton and kaon-proton resonances

Words: 62
Meson-baryon scattering OurBigBook.com
The π+p channel has baryon number one, strangeness zero and I3​=3/2, matching the ordinary uuu Delta baryon. The K+p channel has strangeness plus one, which no three-light-quark baryon can have because each strange quark contributes minus one. A resonance in that channel would require exotic content such as four quarks and an antiquark; the ordinary low-energy qqq multiplets therefore explain the contrast.

Pion-nucleon octet channels (πN→πN,η8​N,KΛ,KΣ)

Words: 43
Meson-baryon scattering OurBigBook.com
For an initial pion-nucleon state and outgoing meson octet-baryon octet pair, conservation of baryon number and strangeness allows πN, η8​N, KΛ, and KΣ, subject to electric charge and production thresholds. Total isospin is 1/2 or 3/2; the η8​N and KΛ channels contain only 1/2.

Weak interaction

Words: 4k Articles: 35
Standard Model OurBigBook.com
The weak interaction changes particle species through the charged current and also acts through the neutral current. Familiar examples include beta-minus decay and neutrino scattering. It is short-range and chiral: its W boson and Z boson couplings distinguish chirality. Above the electroweak scale it belongs to the unbroken SU(2)L​×U(1)Y​ electroweak interaction. At much lower energies, W boson exchange is approximated by the Fermi interaction.
A particularly direct window into the weak interaction is the Wu experiment: a sample with oriented nuclear spins emits electrons preferentially toward one end of its spin axis. The comparison tests parity conservation, because spin is an axial vector and momentum is a polar vector. The polarized beta-decay angular distribution translates that geometric distinction into a measurable counting asymmetry.

Weak radiative hyperon decay

Words: 60
Weak interaction OurBigBook.com
A hyperon decay that changes quark flavour while emitting a photon. An example is Ξ0→Λγ, which changes strangeness and cannot be purely electromagnetic. Its amplitude can contain short-distance loops and long-distance hadronic contributions. photon attachments to a weak quark-exchange graph must be completed consistently with electromagnetic gauge invariance. A quark topology identifies allowed flavour flow but does not by itself calculate a reliable hadronic rate.

Sargent's rule (Γ∝GF2​Q5)

Words: 69
Weak interaction OurBigBook.com
In a low-energy allowed weak three-body decay, negligible final-state masses and a nearly constant effective matrix element give a fifth-power energy-release dependence. For muon decay in natural units, Γ≃GF2​mμ5​/(192π3). This four-fermion approximation requires momentum transfers small compared with the W boson mass. Extrapolation to a heavy particle able to emit a real W changes the decay kinematics and the mass scaling, so it is not a reliable heavy-particle lifetime prediction.

Second-order strangeness-changing weak decay (∣ΔS∣=2)

Words: 87
Weak interaction OurBigBook.com
A decay amplitude changing strangeness by two units requires at least two insertions of the low-energy weak interaction in the Standard Model. Each charged-current insertion can remove only one net strange quark in such a process. Both two-W boson tree topologies and loop contributions can occur; a loop is not required for every exclusive final state. At hadronic energies, the extra power of the Fermi constant, with the needed powers of an energy scale to balance units, strongly suppresses a second-order amplitude relative to a first-order one. This is distinct from Cabibbo suppression within a fixed weak order.

Parity violation

Words: 1k Articles: 6
Weak interaction OurBigBook.com
Parity violation means that a physical law fails to be invariant under the spatial reflection represented by the parity operator. A process and its fully inverted counterpart can then have different probabilities. For beta-minus decay with polarized parent atomic nuclei, a nonzero correlation between nuclear spin and emitted electron momentum is such a test. Rotational symmetry alone allows this correlation: a pseudoscalar is unchanged by proper rotations but changes sign under spatial reflection.

Goldhaber experiment

Words: 56
Parity violation OurBigBook.com
The experiment infers neutrino helicity from nuclear nuclear resonance fluorescence and photon helicity. A spin-zero nucleus undergoes electron capture to a spin-one daughter, which emits a nuclear gamma ray to a spin-zero ground state. Selecting emission along the daughter recoil relates the normalized daughter, photon and neutrino helicities. Reversing magnetized iron measures the circular polarization of the selected radiation.[ref]

Lee-Yang proposal for a parity test

Words: 115
Parity violation OurBigBook.com
In 1956, Tsung-Dao Lee and Chen Ning Yang examined the evidence for parity conservation in the weak interaction. Their paper, Question of Parity Conservation in Weak Interactions, distinguished an untested assumption from an established experimental result and proposed comparing electron emission along opposite directions relative to oriented nuclear spins, explicitly considering cobalt-60. It proposed a test; it did not report the later Wu experiment.[ref]
The conceptual improvement is the choice of observable. An angle between two polar vectors is preserved by spatial reflection; its distribution can conceal parity violation. An angle between an axial vector and a polar vector changes to its supplement. Thus a spin-resolved directional measurement asks a different question from an unpolarized total decay rate.

Wu experiment

Words: 287
Parity violation OurBigBook.com
The Wu experiment was performed by Chien-Shiung Wu, Ernest Ambler, Raymond Webster Hayward, Dale D. Hoppes, and Ralph Percy Hudson; its 1957 report was Experimental Test of Parity Conservation in Beta Decay. Their experiment supplied the evidence that the Lee-Yang proposal for a parity test had called for.[ref]
A cobalt-60 surface layer on a cerium magnesium nitrate crystal was cooled by adiabatic demagnetization; a solenoid's magnetic field polarized its atomic nuclei. An internal anthracene counter detected electrons by particle scintillation; a light pipe carried flashes to a photomultiplier. Polar and equatorial gamma ray counters monitored nuclear polarization and effective temperature; bulk thermometry could miss surface heating.[ref]
Reversing nuclear polarization reversed the electron excess; warming erased it with gamma ray anisotropy. Warm rates were field-independent. Cooling-field reversal checked remanence; poorly polarized sources checked magnetic deflection. Electrons favored the direction opposite spin.[ref]
The gamma ray anisotropy diagnoses the preparation; the electron asymmetry diagnoses parity violation. These are different jobs. A directionally uneven gamma ray signal alone need not violate parity conservation: a distribution even in the cosine of the angle can distinguish an axis from its perpendicular without distinguishing its two ends. The spin-momentum correlation instead distinguishes those ends.
The inference requires control of changes in detection efficiency, electron transport and nuclear polarization. Neutral current

Weak interaction OurBigBook.com
The weak neutral current couples the Z boson to a fermion without changing its electric charge. Its vector and axial-vector coefficients depend on weak isospin, electric charge, and the weak mixing angle.
The neutral current transfers no electric charge at a fermion vertex; “neutral” does not mean that every participating particle is uncharged. For example, νμ​e−→νμ​e− transfers energy and momentum to an electron through Z boson exchange. By contrast, a charged current can convert a muon neutrino into a muon, as in νμ​n→μ−p. Both processes conserve total electric charge. A photon also carries no electric charge, but an active neutrino has no electromagnetic charge coupling: its neutral current is a distinct weak interaction.
The experimentally useful contrast on a nucleon target is
νμ​+N⟶μ−+X(charged current),νμ​+N⟶νμ​+X(neutral current),
(14)
where N is a nucleon and X is an allowed final state of hadrons. The charged current makes a charged lepton available for identification; the outgoing neutrino in a neutral current leaves no bubble-chamber track. A sample of hadronic events without an identified muon therefore poses an experimental question: how many could instead be neutron interactions, or charged current events whose muon was missed? The answer requires a detector-response and background analysis, not merely an inspection for an absent line.

Gargamelle was a heavy-liquid bubble chamber at CERN. Its 1973 collaboration report, Observation of neutrino-like interactions without muon or electron in the Gargamelle neutrino experiment, by F. J. Hasert and colleagues, described hadronic events with no identified muon or electron and evaluated rates relative to charged current events. This is evidence for a neutral current, rather than direct production or photography of a Z boson.[ref]
CERN's Gargamelle account identifies the target liquid as CF3​Br and distinguishes hadronic events from the separate isolated-electron signal. The latter is an antineutrino transferring momentum to an electron, whose electromagnetic particle shower supplies visible tracks. These are different final states, not two names for one event.[ref]
A neutrino beam uses protons striking a target to produce charged pions and kaons; focusing selects parents that undergo particle decay in flight. Their neutrinos pass through shielding into the target. Scanning photographs locates vertices and classifies outgoing tracks.[ref]
Expansion prepares a bubble chamber's superheated liquid; ionization by charged secondaries seeds bubbles for photography.[ref]
The recorded light reveals bubbles, not a directly visible incoming or outgoing neutrino. Reconstructing a vertex and classifying bubble-chamber tracks connects that optical record to a hypothesis about a particle interaction.
The collaboration compared samples with matched hadronic cuts. A flat longitudinal vertex distribution resembled neutrino interactions, but sideways neutrons and multi-step cascades could also flatten it. The background estimate combined visible parent-interaction/secondary-neutron pairs with a cascade calculation including surrounding material. Later proton exposures tested the predicted cascade lengths. Escaping charged hadrons could imitate muons; there was no independent perfect muon tag.[ref]
The inference combines positive evidence for an interaction with controlled alternatives for its visible final state. Shielding suppresses unwanted beam components, yet interactions in surrounding material can generate secondary neutrons; shielding alone cannot certify a neutral current. Nor does a successful neutral current search by itself establish every coupling or the Higgs mechanism. Its importance for the electroweak interaction is that the theory predicts an additional weak channel, with coupling relations that further cross section measurements can test.

The singlet axial U(1)A​ has a chiral anomaly, while the nonsinglet chiral symmetry and vector baryon number remain exact quantum symmetries, up to their shared discrete identifications. Deep inelastic scattering

Words: 1k Articles: 21
Quantum chromodynamics OurBigBook.com
Scattering that resolves the constituents of a hadron at large spacelike momentum transfer, with an inclusive sum over final hadron states.
In electron scattering from a proton, write the reaction as e−p→e−X: the outgoing electron is measured, while X denotes all allowed final hadron states. Large momentum transfer supplies a short-distance probe; a large final invariant mass separates the deep continuum from elastic scattering and individual particle resonances. The useful surprise is that an extended proton can have a response characteristic of much smaller constituents. Deep inelastic scattering turns measurements outside the proton into constraints on its internal parton distribution functions.
The SLAC-MIT deep inelastic electron scattering experiment connects this definition to an actual measurement. Its evidence came from distributions of outgoing electron energies and scattering angles, rather than a photograph of a quark. Bjorken scaling concerns deep-inelastic structure functions after known scattering factors have been accounted for; it does not say that the raw differential scattering cross-section is constant.

SLAC-MIT deep inelastic electron scattering experiment

Words: 712 Articles: 3
Deep inelastic scattering OurBigBook.com
Starting in 1967, a collaboration at the Stanford Linear Accelerator Center and the Massachusetts Institute of Technology directed an electron beam at liquid hydrogen, providing proton targets. Jerome Isaac Friedman, Henry Way Kendall and Richard Edward Taylor participated in this experimental program.[ref]
The 1969 paper Observed Behavior of Highly Inelastic Electron-Proton Scattering reports inclusive electron spectra at 6∘ and 10∘ with incident energies from 7 to 17GeV. Its scaling comparison estimated νlab​W2​ under a transverse-virtual photon assumption, finding approximate agreement as a function of ω=1/x for Q2>1GeV2 and ω>4. These are the paper's conditions, not a claim of exact Bjorken scaling at every momentum transfer.[ref]
SLAC-MIT spectrometer readout and corrections
Words: 145
SLAC-MIT deep inelastic electron scattering experiment OurBigBook.com
A movable magnetic spectrometer selected scattered electrons by momentum and scattering angle. Magnetic fields dispersed momenta at the focal plane. With relativistic electrons, the inferred momentum determines outgoing energy E′. Commissioning included steering the beam through the spectrometer at zero angle to check its optics and accepted solid angle. Counters sorted events into momentum and angle bins. The acceptance entered the conversion from counts to differential scattering cross-sections.[ref]
Radiative corrections matter because photon emission can move events from an elastic scattering peak into lower outgoing-energy bins. The analyses subtracted the elastic radiative tail before unfolding inelastic radiation. Independent MIT and SLAC procedures provided a check. An uncorrected low-E′ tail alone therefore cannot establish deep inelastic scattering.[ref]

Work in natural units with c=1, neglect the electron mass, and put the initial proton at rest with mass M. Let k and k′ be the initial and final electron four-momenta, q=k−k′, and Q2=−q2>0. Define the laboratory energy transfer νlab​=E−E′=P⋅q/M. This νlab​ has units of energy; the invariant P⋅q has units of energy squared. The Bjorken scaling variable and the final hadron invariant mass obey
Q2=4EE′sin2(θ/2),x=2Mνlab​Q2​,W2=(P+q)2=M2+Q2(x1​−1).
(19)
These follow by squaring k−k′ and P+q, using k2=k′2=0 and P=(M,0). Solving the Bjorken x definition gives the outgoing energy and then the scattering angle:
E′=E−2MxQ2​,sin22θ​=4E(E−Q2/(2Mx))Q2​.
(20)
Alternatively, substituting Q2=4EE′sin2(θ/2) before solving gives E′=E/[1+2Esin2(θ/2)/(Mx)]. A chosen x,E,Q2 must satisfy E′>0 and 0≤sin2(θ/2)≤1. In addition, W must exceed the lightest allowed inelastic hadron threshold; positive W2 alone is insufficient.
For an original numerical example, take M=0.938GeV, x=0.3, E=15GeV and Q2=3GeV2. Then νlab​≃5.330GeV, E′≃9.670GeV, θ≃8.25∘, and W≃2.807GeV. Varying 2≤Q2/GeV2≤5 and 10≤E/GeV≤20 at this same Bjorken x keeps every setting physical and gives W2>5.54GeV2, above the proton-pion threshold and the stricter chosen continuum selection W>2GeV. These are calculated settings, not historical measurements.

Quantum chromodynamics predicts departures from exact Bjorken scaling; finite hadron masses also limit the idealization.

Neither curve is measured data or a fit to the SLAC-MIT experiment.
The experimental interpretation required more than a flat curve. The angular dependence and small longitudinal response supported spin one-half partons, expressed at leading order by the Callan-Gross relation F2​=2xF1​. Identification with fractionally charged quarks also drew on later electron, muon and neutrino comparisons. One measured function cannot independently fix all these quantities. Confinement also explains why an inclusive final hadron state need not contain an isolated outgoing quark.

Electroweak interaction

Words: 5k Articles: 76
Standard Model OurBigBook.com
The electroweak interaction is the SU(2)L​×U(1)Y​ gauge theory that unifies the weak and electromagnetic interactions.
An instructive tension motivates the unification: the photon is massless, while the W boson and Z boson are massive; electromagnetic interaction and weak interaction also have different observed low-energy strengths and chiral couplings. A gauge theory can relate their interactions while the Higgs field gives different masses after electroweak symmetry breaking. The resulting theory predicts relationships between processes, not merely a common name for observed phenomena.
Its useful organizing principle is the combination of weak isospin and hypercharge. The surviving electromagnetic generator is Q=T3​+Y in the convention used here. The photon and Z boson are different mixtures of neutral gauge fields, while the charged current uses the charged combinations. The electroweak doublet gauge-boson mass matrix explains why one neutral mixture stays massless. At low energies, a massive W boson propagator instead produces the approximate Fermi interaction, with
2​GF​​=8mW2​g2​=2v21​,mW​=2gv​.
(23)
Here g is the SU(2)L​ gauge coupling and v the Higgs doublet vacuum expectation value. The inverse squared mediator mass suppresses low-energy weak rates. Unification does not require setting g equal to the electromagnetic coupling e: their relation is e=gsinθW​.
A striking experimental consequence is a neutral current in addition to the familiar charged current. The Gargamelle experiment tests this extra channel through visible charged secondaries, with a background problem fundamentally different from directly identifying a Z boson. The muon-neutrino electron recoil spectrum shows how the same Weinberg angle enters another process quantitatively.

It also stresses its unresolved mass problem: symmetry-breaking masses had been inserted, rather than generated by the Higgs mechanism. Establishing the gauge structure and explaining the gauge boson masses were complementary steps.[ref]
Steven Weinberg's A Model of Leptons (1967) builds a spontaneously broken gauge theory for the electron-type leptons, using a scalar doublet to give masses while retaining a massless photon. It derives neutral and charged couplings and discusses neutrino-electron scattering. Its closing question about renormalizability is explicitly unresolved; the paper is neither a proof of that property nor a complete treatment of quarks.[ref]
Abdus Salam's 1979 lecture, Gauge Unification of Fundamental Forces, describes his and Steven Weinberg's completion of the spontaneously broken SU(2)×U(1) formulation for leptons. He separates that construction from the subsequent establishment of renormalizability. Its role is to connect the mass mechanism with predictive neutral and charged couplings, not to identify a photographed event. The Gargamelle evidence subsequently tested the predicted neutral current.[ref]

The Standard Model Higgs field is a complex SU(2)L​ doublet of hypercharge 1/2. Its nonzero vacuum expectation value triggers the Higgs mechanism.
The Higgs field is a scalar field: its components carry internal weak isospin and hypercharge, but no spacetime spin. A complex Higgs doublet contains four real field components. The vacuum expectation value is a property of the lowest-energy state, not a gas of Higgs bosons. A Higgs boson is an excitation about that state.
Why introduce this field? A bare mass term for a gauge field generally fails to respect the local gauge symmetry. A bare Dirac mass term for a charged Standard Model fermion also joins left- and right-handed fields with different Standard Model representations. A Higgs doublet permits gauge-invariant interactions whose expansion about a nonzero vacuum expectation value supplies both masses and definite Higgs boson interactions. The field therefore links the mass problem to experimentally testable coupling relations, as illustrated by the Higgs boson coupling to Z bosons.

In the Higgs mechanism, gauge fields associated with broken generators acquire longitudinal polarizations and masses by absorbing Goldstone modes. Gauge fields of the unbroken subgroup remain massless.
The phrase “absorbing” describes a rearrangement of degrees of freedom, not a collision in which a gauge boson swallows another particle. The gauge symmetry remains a redundancy of the description. A chosen vacuum expectation value leaves a smaller subgroup manifest, while gauge-invariant observables describe the physical masses.
A one-field calculation isolates the mechanism. In an Abelian Higgs model, write a complex scalar field locally as Φ=(v+H)eiθ/2​, use Dμ​=∂μ​−ieAμ​, and define Bμ​=Aμ​−∂μ​θ/e. Then

The second term contains a Proca field mass mB​=ev and its interactions with the radial Higgs boson. A local gauge transformation removes θ from the scalar field but leaves its information in the longitudinal vector polarization. The electroweak symmetry breaking calculation applies this idea to three broken directions.

The ATLAS experiment and CMS experiment searched proton-proton collisions at the Large Hadron Collider at collision energies of 7 and 8TeV. Its July 2012 paper reported a combined local statistical significance of 6.0 standard deviations near 126.5GeV; this paper result is distinct from the initial 4 July announcement.[ref]
The CMS experiment used silicon tracking in a 3.8T solenoid, lead-tungstate electromagnetic calorimeters and external muon chambers. Electrons combine tracks and particle showers; muons combine tracking and chamber hits; photons supply shower energies and directions. Selected H→γγ and H→ZZ∗→4ℓ candidates, with ℓ=e,μ, yielded invariant mass peaks. It checked lepton efficiencies with Z boson decays, estimated fake-lepton backgrounds from control samples with relaxed identification, and fitted the smooth diphoton background from data. Its combined local statistical significance was 5.0 standard deviations near 125GeV.[ref]
The ATLAS experiment compared signal-plus-background and background-only hypotheses with a profile likelihood, accounting for systematic uncertainties and correlations between decay channels. Diphoton and four-lepton candidates gave precise invariant masses; WW∗ decays supplied additional evidence with poorer mass reconstruction because of escaping neutrinos. A local p-value concerns one specified mass; scanning masses requires a look-elsewhere effect correction.[ref]
Two-photon decay excludes spin one under the usual assumptions, but does not prove spin zero. A mass peak does not determine every Higgs boson coupling. Production rates, branching fractions and angular correlations require additional tests.[ref]

SPEAR Mark I tau discovery experiment (1975)

Tau (particle) OurBigBook.com
Counterrotating electron and Positron beams at SPEAR collided inside the Mark I magnetic particle detector. Lead–scintillator scintillation counters identified electrons through large shower pulses; small pulses plus hits beyond the iron return identified muons.[ref]
The selection required opposite-charge electron–muon tracks, no detected photons, momenta above 0.65GeV/c, and transverse noncoplanarity above 20∘. Multitrack hadron samples calibrated momentum-dependent misidentification; collinear lepton pairs checked identification losses. Photon and charge control samples tested backgrounds. Acceptance corrections depended on the proposed signal.[ref]
The 1975 claim was anomalous events without a conventional explanation; new-particle pair production was a possible interpretation.[ref] Martin Lewis Perl's lecture describes subsequent evidence for a charged lepton.[ref]
The particle identification problem matters as much as the apparent missing four-momentum in electron-positron collisions. A penetrating hadron can imitate a muon; a particle shower can imitate an electron; an undetected photon or a detector gap can imitate invisible recoil. An absence of additional recorded signals is conditional on detection efficiency. In a proposed signal model, the selected count has the schematic form
Nselected​=Lσε+Nbackground​,
(42)
where L is integrated collider luminosity, σ a cross section, and ε the combined acceptance and detection efficiency. A single count cannot determine all three factors. A control sample must probe the relevant momentum and angular range; its abundant events do not automatically calibrate a differently distributed signal.

Its v6 term is g4v6 when the tree sextic coupling vanishes. The local pole then requires both wavefunction renormalization and a scalar mass counterterm.

Tree scattering in Yukawa theory (Lint​=−gψˉ​ϕψ)

Yukawa interaction OurBigBook.com
For a real scalar coupled through −gψˉ​ϕψ, the scalar-fermion Feynman vertex is −ig. Two-fermion scattering has scalar exchange in the t and u channels with a relative minus from exchanging identical external fermions. Fermion-antifermion scattering has t exchange and s annihilation, again with a relative fermionic minus for a fixed state ordering. Fermion-scalar scattering has the two orderings along one open fermion line, using internal momenta p1​+p2​ and p1​−p4​; these have the same sign. The Mandelstam variables specify the propagator denominators.
Tree scattering with pseudoscalar exchange (V=−igγ5)

Tree scattering in Yukawa theory OurBigBook.com
The pseudoscalar Yukawa interaction with coefficient −g has the displayed Feynman vertex. Its two-fermion tree-level Feynman diagrams are the t and u exchanges; antisymmetry of the final identical fermions requires their relative minus. Fermion-antifermion scattering has t exchange and s annihilation, again with a relative minus. With initial and final states ordered as b1†​d2†​∣0⟩ and b3†​d4†​∣0⟩, the normal-ordered current contributes −d†dvˉγ5v in the exchange channel but db and b†d† in the annihilation channel. These fermionic signs fix the overall sign as well as their interference; changing an external-state phase changes both terms together.

Gauge-invariant electron Yukawa mass (me​=∣ye​∣v/2​)

Words: 49
Yukawa interaction OurBigBook.com
The Standard Model lepton doublet L=(νL​,eL​)T has hypercharge −1/2, the electron singlet eR​ has −1, and the Higgs doublet has 1/2. Therefore −ye​LˉϕeR​+h.c. is gauge-invariant even though a bare eˉL​eR​ mass is not. The vacuum expectation value generates a Dirac mass ∣ye​∣v/2​. In unitary gauge, the Higgs boson coupling is −(me​/v)heˉe after rephasing the electron.

Pseudoscalar Yukawa interaction (igψˉ​γ5ψϕ)

Words: 205 Articles: 2
Yukawa interaction OurBigBook.com
A pseudoscalar Yukawa interaction couples a Dirac field bilinear containing the chirality matrix to a spin-zero field. In the standard mostly-minus gamma matrix convention with γ5=iγ0γ1γ2γ3 and the usual Dirac adjoint, igψˉ​γ5ψϕ is Hermitian for real g and real ϕ. If ϕ is a pseudoscalar, the interaction also preserves parity symmetry in quantum field theory; if ϕ is parity even, it breaks that symmetry. Moving the factor i into the definition of γ5 changes the displayed vertex coefficient but not the interaction. Each vertex has one bosonic leg and two oppositely oriented fermion legs, and preserves Dirac fermion number conservation.
Parity restriction on renormalizable pseudoscalar Yukawa counterterms (Lct​⊃ϕ4,Lct​⊃ϕ,ϕ3)
Words: 50
Pseudoscalar Yukawa interaction OurBigBook.com
For an unbroken parity symmetry in quantum field theory with ϕ a pseudoscalar, pure-scalar local counterterms of mass dimension at most four are even in ϕ. A four-vertex fermion loop requires a quartic counterterm, even when the initial Lagrangian density shows only a Yukawa interaction. The one-point and three-point pure-boson vertices vanish at all orders: their available external four-momenta cannot form a parity-odd Lorentz scalar.
Hermiticity of a pseudoscalar Dirac bilinear ((ψˉ​γ5ψ)†=−ψˉ​γ5ψ)
Words: 71
Pseudoscalar Yukawa interaction OurBigBook.com
With the usual Dirac adjoint, Hermitian γ5 and {γ0,γ5}=0, taking the adjoint gives ψ†γ5γ0ψ=−ψ†γ0γ5ψ. Consequently a real pseudoscalar with coupling −gϕψˉ​γ5ψ has a Hermitian interaction only if g∗=−g. Writing g=igP​ with real gP​ gives the familiar interaction −igP​ϕψˉ​γ5ψ. Formal Euler-Lagrange field equations obtained with independent spinor and adjoint variables can still be computed for the original symbolic coupling; it must not silently be identified with a real physical coupling.

Fermion mass matrix (−fˉ​L​Mf​fR​+h.c.)

Words: 39
Yukawa interaction OurBigBook.com
After a scalar vacuum expectation value, a Yukawa matrix produces a bilinear −fˉ​L​Mf​fR​+h.c.. Independent unitary left/right rotations diagonalize Mf​ with nonnegative masses. Extra scalar-dependent operators can make the physical scalar coupling matrix fail to diagonalize with the mass matrix.

Yukawa matrix (Yf​)

Words: 180 Articles: 2
Yukawa interaction OurBigBook.com
A Yukawa matrix contains the flavor-space couplings between left-handed fermions, right-handed fermions, and a scalar field. Its singular values determine fermion masses after symmetry breaking, while mismatches between its diagonalizing transformations produce flavor mixing.
S3-invariant Yukawa matrix for a doublet and a sign singlet (λ=diag(a,a,b))
Words: 95
Yukawa matrix OurBigBook.com
Let the left and right fermions transform in D⊕ε, where D is the two-dimensional irreducible representation of the symmetric group S3​ and ε is the sign representation. Let the scalar field be a trivial representation. In matching orthonormal bases, invariance of ψˉ​L​λψR​ says that λ commutes with D⊕ε. The Schur lemma forces each diagonal irreducible block to be scalar and both mixed blocks to vanish, giving the displayed form. Thus after a vacuum expectation value h, the physical fermion mass matrix has singular values ∣ha∣,∣ha∣,∣hb∣: unbroken S3​ enforces a degenerate doublet. In a common nonorthonormal basis with invariant Gram matrix K, the doublet coefficient is aK; canonical normalization recovers aI2​.
Charged-lepton Yukawa matrix diagonalization (UL†​Yℓ​UR​=diag(ye​,yμ​,yτ​))
Words: 51
Yukawa matrix OurBigBook.com
A singular value decomposition of the charged-lepton Yukawa matrix uses independent unitary rotations of left- and right-handed leptons. Their gauge-covariant kinetic terms are unchanged because each rotation mixes identical Standard Model representations. After electroweak symmetry breaking, the nonnegative singular values give Dirac masses mi​=yi​v/2​ and diagonal Higgs boson couplings mi​/v. When the neutrinos are massless, rotating their left-handed fields with the charged partners preserves the diagonal weak charged current.

Cabibbo-Kobayashi-Maskawa matrix (VCKM​)

Words: 2k Articles: 12
Standard Model fermion OurBigBook.com
The Cabibbo-Kobayashi-Maskawa matrix V=UuL†​UdL​ compares the left-handed unitary matrices that diagonalize the up-type and down-type Yukawa matrices. Its rows label up quarks, charm quarks and top quarks; its columns label down quarks, strange quarks and bottom quarks. In the weak charged current, the coefficient of uˉLi​γμdLj​Wμ+​ is Vij​. A single CKM matrix therefore connects quark masses, flavour-changing decay amplitudes, and CP violation.
Write sij​=sinθij​ and cij​=cosθij​. An exactly unitary matrix with three mixing angles and one CP-violating phase is
V=​c12​c13​−s12​c23​−c12​s23​s13​eiδs12​s23​−c12​c23​s13​eiδ​s12​c13​c12​c23​−s12​s23​s13​eiδ−c12​s23​−s12​c23​s13​eiδ​s13​e−iδs23​c13​c23​c13​​​.
(51)
This convention agrees with Makoto Kobayashi's account of three-generation quark mixing.[ref]
The Christenson-Cronin-Fitch-Turlay kaon CP violation experiment established the phenomenon that required an explanation. Makoto Kobayashi and Toshihide Maskawa showed that two-generation quark mixing cannot supply it, whereas adding a third quark generation permits an irreducible weak phase. Their 1973 paper also considered additional fields as alternative mechanisms; the three-generation conclusion concerns CP violation from the minimal unitary quark mixing mechanism.[ref]
A common weak phase makes CP violation across mesons testable through the BABAR time-dependent CP violation experiment. It does not explain the cosmic baryon asymmetry.[ref]

CKM unitarity triangle (Vud​Vub∗​+Vcd​Vcb∗​+Vtd​Vtb∗​=0)

Words: 212
Cabibbo-Kobayashi-Maskawa matrix OurBigBook.com
Column orthogonality of the CKM matrix gives three complex numbers
a=Vud​Vub∗​,b=Vcd​Vcb∗​,c=Vtd​Vtb∗​,a+b+c=0.
(52)
Drawing these as successive vectors in the complex plane produces a closed triangle. Its area is 21​∣Im(ab∗)∣=∣J∣/2, because unitarity identifies this imaginary quartet with a signed Jarlskog invariant. A nonzero area therefore detects physical CP violation for nondegenerate quark masses.
For a worked example, choose the exact parametrization of the CKM matrix with s12​=1/4, s23​=1/10, s13​=1/100 and δ=π/3. These are illustrative choices, not fitted quark mixing parameters. They give J≃2.085597×10−4. The unscaled triangle has area approximately 1.042799×10−4.
Divide the closure relation by −b, assuming b=0, and define the complex number
z=ρˉ​+iηˉ​=−ba​.
(53)
The normalized triangle has vertices 0,1,z, with z≃0.195376+0.335788i for these choices. Dividing each side by ∣b∣ divides area by ∣b∣2: its area is ∣J∣/(2∣Vcd​Vcb∗​∣2)=∣ηˉ​∣/2, approximately 0.167894. The familiar normalized picture therefore does not itself have area ∣J∣/2.
Under quantum field rephasings, a,b,c all acquire the same phase, so the original triangle merely rotates and z stays fixed. Ratios and angles can thus compare quark mixing measurements without dependence on field conventions. If the Jarlskog invariant vanishes, the triangle collapses; additional quark mass degeneracies require extra care in interpreting the converse.

Wolfenstein parametrization (λ, A, ρ, η)

Words: 164
Cabibbo-Kobayashi-Maskawa matrix OurBigBook.com
The Wolfenstein parametrization organizes the CKM matrix in powers of a small parameter λ=s12​, defining s23​=Aλ2 and s13​eiδ=Aλ3(ρ+iη). Substitution into the exact unitary matrix gives the cubic truncation
V(3)=​1−λ2/2−λAλ3(1−ρ−iη)​λ1−λ2/2−Aλ2​Aλ3(ρ−iη)Aλ21​​.
(54)
This is a useful truncation, with entrywise corrections starting at order λ4, rather than an exactly unitary matrix. For example, its first-row squared norm is 1+λ4/4+A2λ6(ρ2+η2), already different from one. The exact definitions of the sines can instead be inserted into the exact CKM matrix, retaining every cosine, to obtain exact unitarity.
For the illustrative parameters of the CKM unitarity triangle, the exact definitions give λ=1/4, A=8/5, ρ=1/5 and η=3​/5. The first-row norm error in V(3) is 0.0010765625, whereas the exact CKM matrix has unit row norms. To leading order the Jarlskog invariant is J≃A2λ6η, but the exact expression includes cosine factors. The barred parameters ρˉ​,ηˉ​ are defined by the exact ratio in the CKM unitarity triangle; they differ from ρ,η beyond leading order. This distinction matters when a geometrical closure test is used to test unitarity.

Quark rephasing and CP conservation

Words: 270 Articles: 1
Cabibbo-Kobayashi-Maskawa matrix OurBigBook.com
For nondegenerate quark masses, changing the constant quantum phases of quark fields preserves their diagonal mass terms. Adopt the convention
Vij′​=e−iαi​Vij​eiβj​.
(55)
Such quantum field rephasings alter individual entries of the CKM matrix without altering physics. Physical CP symmetry in this mixing sector means that some allowed convention makes the CKM matrix real. Toshihide Maskawa emphasized the distinction between complex entries and an irremovable CP-violating phase.[ref]
Here is a constructive two-generation argument. For a generic 2×2 unitary matrix, use the three effective row/column phases to make V11​,V12​,V22​ real and positive. Column orthogonality then forces V21​ to be real and negative. Row normalization leaves just the real rotation specified by the Cabibbo angle. Zero entries are limiting cases and introduce no weak phase. Thus two-generation quark mixing cannot violate CP symmetry through this mechanism, even when its entries initially look complex.
For three quark generations, the Jarlskog invariant provides an obstruction to repeating that construction: all four phase factors cancel from its defining quartet. If its imaginary part is nonzero, no choice of quantum field rephasings can make every entry real. With nondegenerate quark masses, this proves physical CP violation in the mixing sector. This argument concerns the weak interaction; it does not dispose of the separate Strong CP problem.
CP transformation of a charged quark current (Lcc​(V)CP​Lcc​(V∗))
Words: 92
Quark rephasing and CP conservation OurBigBook.com
Under charge conjugation, uˉγμ(1−γ5)d becomes −dˉγμ(1+γ5)u. Parity reverses the chirality again and applies the Lorentz parity matrix. The minus sign cancels that of charge conjugation on the charged vector field. Thus each charged-current operator is exchanged with its Hermitian conjugate under CP symmetry, giving the displayed transformation for the CKM matrix V. For nondegenerate quark masses, physical CP conservation means that allowed quark rephasings can make V real. A nonzero Jarlskog invariant obstructs this. A merely complex phase convention is not proof of physical CP violation, and V=I is a CP-conserving counterexample to unconditional noninvariance.

CKM parameter counting ((N−1)2)

Words: 102
Cabibbo-Kobayashi-Maskawa matrix OurBigBook.com
An N×N unitary matrix has N2 real parameters. Its real rotation subgroup has N(N−1)/2 mixing angles, leaving N(N+1)/2 phases. The N up-type and N down-type quark fields allow 2N quantum field rephasings, but their common phase acts trivially on the CKM matrix. Removing 2N−1 phases therefore leaves
Nangles​=2N(N−1)​,Nphases​=2(N−1)(N−2)​.
(56)
For two quark generations, there is one mixing angle and no physical CP-violating phase. For three quark generations, there are three mixing angles and one physical CP-violating phase. The count describes generic, nondegenerate quark masses and generic mixing; a vanishing mixing angle can make the remaining phase unobservable, and mass degeneracies enlarge the allowed basis changes. Three quark generations permit CP violation but do not force it.

The Cabibbo angle θC​ describes the real two-generation quark mixing rotation
V=(cosθC​−sinθC​​sinθC​cosθC​​).
(57)
Thus Vud​=Vcs​=cosθC​, Vus​=sinθC​ and Vcd​=−sinθC​. Nicola Cabibbo formulated the mixing of weak charged current couplings before the three-generation mechanism of CP violation; this foundational contribution is distinct from the later extension.[ref]

If two semileptonic decays differ by s→u versus d→u, an equal-hadronic-strength approximation and a fifth-power phase space ansatz give rs​=Ksin2θC​Δs5​ and rd​=Kcos2θC​Δd5​. Their partial decay rates are ri​=Bi​/τi​, where Bi​ is the appropriate branching fraction and τi​ the total mean lifetime. Taking the ratio gives the displayed expression. Different hadronic hadronic form factors, finite electron mass and recoil corrections prevent this simplified extraction from being an exact determination.

Cabibbo angle OurBigBook.com
A small weak charged current amplitude factor associated with sinθC​. A doubly suppressed amplitude contains two such factors, giving a rate suppression of order tan4θC​ relative to a favoured process when other matrix elements are comparable.
Cabibbo hierarchy of neutral-D two-body decays

Cabibbo suppression OurBigBook.com
In the charged-current spectator topology c→qW+, W+→uqˉ​′, the magnitudes of the CKM factors give favoured, singly suppressed and doubly suppressed amplitudes of orders 1, tanθC​ and tan2θC​. Squaring gives rate orders 1, tan2θC​ and tan4θC​. Two singly suppressed channels are not thereby predicted to have equal rates: hadronic matrix elements, phase space and rescattering can differ.

Jarlskog invariant (J)

Words: 140
Cabibbo-Kobayashi-Maskawa matrix OurBigBook.com
The Jarlskog invariant is a measure of CP violation that survives quantum field rephasings. Fix its sign by the quartet
J=Im(Vud​Vcs​Vus∗​Vcd∗​).
(58)
For the exact three-generation CKM matrix, direct multiplication gives
J=c12​c23​c132​s12​s23​s13​sinδ.
(59)
The CKM unitarity triangle's illustrative parameters give J=8999155​/3200000000≃2.085597×10−4. Setting s13​=0 or δ=0 makes J=0: the existence of three quark generations is necessary for this mechanism, but not sufficient for CP violation.
To see the invariance directly, the phases multiplying Vud​Vcs​Vus∗​Vcd∗​ sum to
(−αu​+βd​)+(−αc​+βs​)+(αu​−βs​)+(αc​−βd​)=0.
(60)
Under CP, the CKM matrix is complex conjugated and J changes sign. In an exactly unitary three-generation CKM matrix, quartets formed from any distinct pair of rows and columns have imaginary parts equal to J up to sign. This follows by multiplying a row orthogonality relation by a suitable pair of entries and taking its imaginary part: its diagonal product is real, forcing the two remaining imaginary parts to cancel. The same Jarlskog invariant therefore determines the areas of all six unscaled CKM unitarity triangles.

BABAR time-dependent CP violation experiment

Words: 388 Articles: 1
Cabibbo-Kobayashi-Maskawa matrix OurBigBook.com
BABAR used asymmetric electron-Positron collisions near the Upsilon meson 4S resonance to prepare neutral B meson pairs. It reconstructed one decay into charmonium plus a kaon, and used flavour tagging on the other B meson with charged leptons or kaons. Silicon tracking reconstructed decay vertices for the decay-time difference. Self-tagging decays calibrated mistags and time resolution; charged decays provided a control. The tagged time distributions established CP violation, limited by backgrounds, mistags and vertex alignment.[ref]
The Lorentz boost converts vertex separation to Δt≃Δz/(βboost​γboost​c) at leading order. Unequal beam energies thus make a time difference measurable as a distance.[ref]
Time-dependent neutral-B CP asymmetry (Atag​(Δt)=Ssin(ΔmΔt)−Ccos(ΔmΔt))
Words: 255
BABAR time-dependent CP violation experiment OurBigBook.com
With CPT symmetry, write the propagating states of neutral meson mixing as p∣B0⟩±q∣Bˉ0⟩, defining the coefficient ratio q/p. Let Δm be their mass splitting and use units ℏ=1.
For rates f±​ tagged as B0,Bˉ0 and Δt=tf​−ttag​, neglect the decay width difference and take ∣q/p∣=1. Define
λf​=pq​Af​Aˉf​​,S=1+∣λf​∣22Imλf​​,C=1+∣λf​∣21−∣λf​∣2​.
(61)
Here Af​,Aˉf​ are decay amplitudes. The tagged asymmetry is (f+​−f−​)/(f+​+f−​)=Ssin(ΔmΔt)−Ccos(ΔmΔt) in this convention.[ref]
For a single weak phase in a charmonium-kaon CP eigenstate with eigenvalue ηf​, λf​≃ηf​e−2iβ gives S=−ηf​sin2β, C≃0, with
β=arg(−Vtd​Vtb∗​Vcd​Vcb∗​​).
(62)
This connects the CKM unitarity triangle to quantum interference between direct decay and decay after neutral meson mixing.[ref]
For an independent teaching example choose x=ΔmΔt, λf​=4i/3 and an arbitrary common positive envelope F(Δt). Then S=24/25, C=−7/25 and
f±​=F(Δt)[1±(2524​sinx+257​cosx)].
(63)
Because (24/25)2+(7/25)2=1, both rates remain nonnegative. At x=0, the asymmetry is 7/25; at x=π/2, it is 24/25. These chosen values illustrate the sign convention and are not experimental estimates. More generally S2+C2=1−[2Reλf​/(1+∣λf​∣2)]2≤1.
If a tag flips independently with probability w, exchanging f+​ and f−​ for that fraction of events gives Aobserved​=(1−2w)Atag​ by direct subtraction. The plotted toy choice w=1/5 reduces the amplitude to 3/5 of its ideal value; at w=1/2 the tag contains no flavour information. Finite time resolution additionally averages over nearby oscillation phases. Extracting a weak phase consequently requires calibrated readout as well as a CKM matrix prediction.
